2611.24888v1.title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
2611.24888v1.authors: Muhammad Rizky Wellyanto, Hajara-Yasmin Isa, Kexin Xue, Vishal Ravichandran, Wenpeng Lu, Jerry O. Talton, Ranjitha Kumar
2611.24888v1.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

2611.24833v1.title: DispersedBFT: Bottleneck-Free Primary-Backup Consensus using Dispersed Replication
2611.24833v1.authors: Nancy Kansal, Celine Sana, Jelle Hellings
2611.24833v1.abstract: The advent of blockchains is fueling the development of novel resilient data management systems (RDSs). Typically, these RDSs are managed using a primary-backup design using a consensus protocol such as PBFT. In these primary-backup designs, a single participant, the primary, is responsible for coordinating the replication and execution of requests. Unfortunately, the central role of the primary makes it a bottleneck that drastically limits performance. In this paper, we propose DispersedBFT, a high performance PBFT-like consensus protocol that utilizes dispersed replication to eliminate the primary bottleneck of PBFT-like consensus. In specific, DispersedBFT uses information dispersal to distribute the task of replicating request from the primary to the backups. We propose several variants of DispersedBFT with either low CPU cost (by using Message Authentication Codes and Merkle proofs) or communication cost (by using digital signatures). We practically analyze the performance of DispersedBFT and show it greatly outperforms PBFT and HotStuff: DispersedBFT supports a throughput of 3.4Mtxn/sec with 43 replicas and is up-to 6.2x faster than PBFT and 2.6x faster than HotStuff.

2611.24646v1.title: Conceptual full-vehicle modeling of a modular all-wheel-drive robotic ADS test platform as a foundation for a digital twin architecture
2611.24646v1.authors: Felix Florian Schwald, Martin Meiners, Michael Viehof, Erik Hultman, Edwin Kamau
2611.24646v1.abstract: This paper presents the development of an initial full-vehicle simulation model of the PixKit modular electric test platform in IPG CarMaker. The objective is to create a physics-based and extendable model structure that can serve as a low-level foundation for future digital twin applications. The reference vehicle is a skateboard chassis combining unconventional vehicle characteristics such as four independent wheel-hub motors and rear axle steering capable of high steering angles. Since complete measurement data of the vehicle is not yet available, the model parameterization is based on a combination of manufacturer documentation, derived values and engineering assumptions. The modeling approach focuses on the system-level integration of the main vehicle subsystems rather than on a fully validated representation. The resulting model was assessed through basic driving scenarios with different steering inputs and configurations. The simulations showed stable model behavior and physically plausible interaction between the subsystems. The all-wheel-drive configuration produced symmetric wheel responses in longitudinal driving, while counter-phase rear axle steering increased the yaw response and reduced the simulated turning circle diameter compared with front axle steering only. The circular driving scenario further indicated bounded roll and slip behavior. Overall, the implemented CarMaker model provides a traceable and functional simulation basis for the PixKit vehicle. It can support future model refinement, calibration with real vehicle data and development with the goal of creating a validated digital twin architecture.

2611.24624v1.title: Instanton tunnelling as a verifiable benchmark for digital quantum simulation: circuit structure, classical simulability and hardware reproducibility
2611.24624v1.abstract: We use instanton-mediated tunnelling in the quartic double well as a benchmark for digital quantum simulation that is checkable against an exact answer at every step. The instanton enters through the classical analysis; the hardware tests the dynamics of the lattice model. A unary (single-excitation) encoding maps N lattice sites to N qubits, with the single-excitation dynamics as a reference that remains classically cheap at any N. For a second-order Trotter circuit with adjacent, equal-angle XX/YY pairs on each bond, we prove that the Schmidt rank across any cut is at most four at every gate boundary and at most two after each pair, independently of N. Matrix-product-state simulations of this gate list reproduce the exact splitting up to N = 48. For this bond-wise formula the admissible Trotter step shrinks roughly as N^-2, so one tunnelling period costs about N^3.3 two-qubit gates; a kinetic/potential splitting keeps the step near 0.065 up to N=128, so this scaling belongs to splitting the kinetic term bond by bond. At a coarser, separately bounded step we measure the full transfer at N=8 on two superconducting processors, recovering the lattice splitting to a few percent and its dependence on the barrier height, which at this resolution is set by the lattice rather than by the instanton. Over 9 repetitions, runs taken minutes apart agree to shot noise, while runs hours to weeks apart differ by up to 6.1%, also on a fixed set of qubits; with sessions as the sampling unit, the processors differ in the damping, while a difference in the splitting is not established. Normalising by the measured single-excitation population extends the usable depth about 4-fold but does not improve the splitting. A Gaussian start state, which needs no diagonalisation, reproduces the splitting of the eigenvector-based start to within 1.6 percentage points.

2611.24591v1.title: Reliable arithmetic circuits using less reliable (sub-digital) logic
2611.24591v1.authors: Trevor McCourt, Ila R. Fiete, Neil Gershenfeld, Isaac L. Chuang
2611.24591v1.abstract: The frequent static failure of CMOS logic gates at ultra-low voltages has historically been perceived as a strict barrier to extreme voltage scaling: this paper introduces a statistical circuit law proving this intuition wrong. We discovered a universal power law connecting gate and circuit static failure probabilities, revealing that circuit failure requires the simultaneous breakdown of an entire gate cluster rather than a single component. Because the required cluster size increases rapidly as voltage drops, low-voltage \textit{sub-digital} logic exhibits surprising inherent resilience to static failure. This insight stems from new theoretical tools we developed to quantify static failure, extending well beyond conventional voltage-margin analysis. Consequently, sub-digital processors could potentially offer a viable, near-term solution to drastically reduce the energy demands of AI.

2611.24565v1.title: Beyond Appearance: Evidence-Guided Programmatic 3D Scene Reconstruction with Agentic Lighting Reasoning
2611.24565v1.authors: Zeting Luo, Yifan Li, Shuai Yang
2611.24565v1.abstract: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.

2611.24411v1.title: Long-distance continuous variable entanglement distribution over deployed fibre
2611.24411v1.authors: Huy Q. Nguyen, Benjamin L. Larsen, Luiz C. C. P. Filho, Yijian Meng, Mikael Ø. Lassen, Jonas S. Neergaard-Nielsen, Tobias Gehring, Ulrik L. Andersen, Adnan A. E. Hajomer
2611.24411v1.abstract: Continuous-variable (CV) entanglement offers deterministic generation and room-temperature coherent detection for quantum networks, but distributing it over deployed fibre has been hindered by the need to stabilise optical phase, polarisation, and timing at remote receivers. Here we demonstrate, to our knowledge, the first distribution of CV entanglement over deployed metropolitan fibre using independent coherent receivers. The two modes of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state are delivered to remote nodes through 23 km ($\approx 7$ dB loss) and 450 m ($\approx 1$ dB loss) deployed fibre links. Each node uses its own free-running laser and polarisation-diverse coherent receiver. Co-propagating pilot tones enable digital recovery of timing, phase and polarisation, while inter-mode correlations fix the quadrature alignment. We certify entanglement with a Simon-Duan value of $1.915\pm 0.013$, below the separability bound of 2 and a logarithmic negativity of $0.067\pm0.011$. By replacing optical stabilisation with digital reconstruction, our approach offers a practical route towards scalable CV quantum networks.

2611.24392v1.title: Mesh Sensitivity of Different Boundary Treatments in High-Order Compact Gas-Kinetic Scheme for Hypersonic Heat-Flux Prediction
2611.24392v1.authors: Xingyi Jiang, Jiawang Zhang, Junlei Mu, Xing Ji
2611.24392v1.abstract: Accurate wall-heat-flux prediction in hypersonic flow depends on both the wall treatment and the available near-wall resolution. This work compares three complete implementations of a gas-kinetic scheme (GKS) for Mach~8.03 laminar flow over an isothermal circular cylinder: a linear Green--Gauss scheme (GG), a compact ghost-cell scheme (GC), and a pointwise one-sided compact scheme (POS). In POS, the stationary isothermal-wall conditions are imposed at the two Gaussian points used by the kinetic wall-flux quadrature. A reference mesh and six meshes in the uniform reduction (UR), log-layer unpacked (LLU), and log-layer packed (LLP) families are used to assess heat-flux sensitivity. At 24 digitized experimental angles, GG has the lowest root-mean-square difference on the reference, UR, and LLP families, whereas POS is closest on the two LLU meshes; GC is not the lowest-RMS scheme on any tested mesh. Hence no treatment is uniformly superior. On the present high-aspect-ratio cylinder grids, GG is the more robust choice except under LLU node redistribution, for which POS is preferable. Uniform reduction produces the largest heat-flux response for all three implementations. The comparison concerns complete schemes and does not isolate the pointwise constraints from differences in reconstruction and geometry representation.

2611.24350v1.title: Theses by publication in Spain: output, authorship and integrity concerns
2611.24350v1.authors: Álvaro Cabezas-Clavijo, Nazaret Barriga, Rafael Repiso
2611.24350v1.abstract: Theses by publication are accepted in most Spanish universities, yet there is little empirical evidence on the scientific output that supports them or on the role doctoral candidates play in that output, and it is not even possible to determine what share of all theses defended in the country follow this format. To address this gap, we analysed a sample of 338 theses by publication defended in Spain in 2025 and 2026, identified in the Teseo database and downloaded in full text. On average, each thesis included 4.0 works, of which 3.0 were articles indexed in Scopus, and 61.1% of these articles appeared in first-quartile SJR journals. The doctoral candidate was first author in 81.1% of the articles and held an intermediate position in 12.1%, while 17 candidates (5.4%) were not first or sole author of any article in their compendium. As for publication venues, MDPI was the main publisher, with 23.2% of the articles, and 40.6% of the candidates published at least one work from their compendium with it. Overall, 45.4% of the candidates used so-called grey publishers, such as MDPI or Frontiers, at least once, and for almost 10% of them these publishers were the only outlet for the compendium. We also detected other infrequent but questionable practices, such as the inclusion of works published in journals delisted from Scopus or in special issues guest-edited by the candidates themselves, works still under review, and articles included in two different theses. Taken together, these results point to the need to clarify regulations on theses by publication, in particular regarding the candidate's authorship of the works linked to the thesis and the quality criteria required of publication venues. Theses by publication should also be identified in a standardised way in official registers, so that they can be retrieved and monitored.

2611.24263v1.title: Design and performance of the front-end readout electronics for LACT
2611.24263v1.authors: Changge Zi, Jinfan Chang, Fengfan Yang, Ming Wei, Wei Wei
2611.24263v1.abstract: The Large Array of Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescope (LACT) will complement the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) with a target angular resolution of 0.05 degrees to resolve the morphology of Very-High-Energy gamma-ray sources. The array is designed to comprise 32 telescopes with 6-meter apertures within LHAASO at an altitude of approximately 4410 meters. Each camera contains 1616 silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). We developed a front-end readout electronics (FEE) board integrating 16 channels of SiPM gain compensation and high-speed waveform sampling for operation at high altitude and over a wide temperature range. The gain compensation circuit independently adjusts the operating voltage of each SiPM according to its temperature and monitors the actual operating voltage. Previous tests of the adopted compensation scheme showed SiPM gain drift below 2% from -20 to 30 degrees Celsius. The waveform sampling circuit uses two 14-bit AC9628 analog-to-digital converters, each operating in eight-channel mode, to digitize the SiPM pulse waveform at 250 million samples per second. The integral nonlinearity of the DC response is 0.0709% over a differential DC voltage range of -950 mV to +950 mV at the AC9628 input. Equivalent electrical pulses with a full width at half maximum of 37.42 ns are used to simulate the SiPM output signals. At a differential pulse amplitude of approximately 237 mV at the AC9628 input, the pulse integral area resolution is 0.2725%. This paper presents the circuit design and performance tests of the FEE for the LACT camera.

2611.24650v1.title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
2611.24650v1.authors: Prakhar Mishra, Bhavya Yajush Awasthi, Tanuja, Nishant
2611.24650v1.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content.We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

2611.24626v1.title: Transferring an analysis of human brain organization to language models
2611.24626v1.authors: Donghyeok Lee, Sangwon Yu, Sangkwon Park, Hye Youn Park, Munyoung Chang, Sungroh Yoon
2611.24626v1.abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.

2611.24597v1.title: DAL: Dynamic Angular Loss for Imbalanced Medical Image Classification
2611.24597v1.authors: Salman Mohammad, Furkan Kasım, Manuel Günther
2611.24597v1.abstract: Class imbalance remains a major obstacle in medical image classification, where rare but clinically important classes are often overshadowed by majority categories. Although current strategies for reducing bias, including angle-based softmax (ABS) losses, offer strong discriminative features, their behavior in settings with a small number of severely imbalanced classes remains insufficiently understood. Previous approaches that estimate the intrinsic parameters of ABS rely on the assumption of many classes, which does not hold in medical settings. We derive data-driven upper and lower bounds for the scale parameter and an upper bound for the angular margin using negative-angle statistics, and use these to drive a batch-adaptive angular margin (BAAM), which we combine with dynamically-weighted cross entropy (DWCE) to define our dynamic angular loss (DAL). Across four highly imbalanced medical image classification benchmarks spanning dermatology, ophthalmology, and gastrointestinal endoscopy, our method consistently achieves superior balanced accuracy and the lowest coefficient of variation of per-class recall. Although this entails a small performance reduction on majority classes, the gains on minority categories are substantial, yielding a reliable and equitable overall classifier. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/msalman95/DAL.

2611.24487v1.title: Unmyelinated axons alter the biological interpretation of MRI biomarkers of demyelination
2611.24487v1.authors: Ali Abdollahzadeh, Ricardo Coronado-Leija, Elizabeth Chasen, Sungheon G. Kim, Dmitry S. Novikov, Els Fieremans
2611.24487v1.abstract: Quantitative MRI methods are widely used to probe white matter microstructure; yet diffusion- and relaxation-based metrics are often interpreted primarily in terms of myelinated axons, implicitly assuming a negligible contribution from unmyelinated axons. Here, combining diffusion MRI (dMRI), relaxation-based MRI, and electron microscopy (EM) in the cuprizone mouse model of demyelination and recovery, we examine how unmyelinated axons shape MRI-derived microstructural indices, including axonal water fraction and $g$-ratio. To enable quantitative cellular-level comparisons, we developed automated tools for instance-level EM segmentation of white matter, allowing morphological analysis of myelinated and unmyelinated axonal populations. We find that, in the mouse model, diffusion-derived estimates of axonal water fraction reflect contributions from both axonal populations at sufficiently short diffusion times; accounting for unmyelinated axons removes an apparent bias and reveals that this metric corresponds to the total intra-axonal space rather than myelinated fibers alone. Similarly, MRI-derived $g$-ratio estimates correlate strongly with EM only when both axonal populations are included. We further demonstrate that within-voxel $g$-ratio heterogeneity introduces a systematic negative bias of up to $8\%$, increasing with the fraction of unmyelinated axons and variability in myelin thickness. Together, these findings change the biological interpretation of MRI biomarkers during demyelination by demonstrating that unmyelinated axons are a major determinant of MRI-derived white matter indices and that combining diffusion and relaxation contrasts enables a more accurate and interpretable quantification of demyelination. They further highlight the need for quantitative biomarkers that account for axonal heterogeneity in both health and disease.

2611.24591v1.authors: Trevor McCourt, Ila R. Fiete, Neil Gershenfeld, Isaac L. Chuang

2611.24565v1.authors: Zeting Luo, Yifan Li, Shuai Yang
2611.24565v1.abstract: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. 2611.24436v1.title: From real to synthetic: PSG-GAN learns sleep apnea signal dynamics for AI training
2611.24436v1.authors: Riku Huttunen, Samu Kainulainen, Matias Rusanen, Sami Myllymaa, Juha Töyräs, Timo Leppänen, Henri Korkalainen
2611.24436v1.abstract: Synthetic polysomnography (PSG) data has great potential in healthcare applications, for example in substituting real data that is sensitive and challenging to collect. Previous research on synthetic PSG data has been largely focused on short segments of individual signals, overlooking the inter-signal dynamics related to sleep disorders. In this study, we developed a generative adversarial network (PSG-GAN) for co-synthesizing longer segments of multiple PSG signals with diverse and complex characteristics typical of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The synthetic signals appeared realistic, and the electroencephalography and electrooculography band powers were similarly distributed across sleep stages. Moreover, the PSG-GAN learned to mirror signal interactions such as changes in photoplethysmography-based heart rate during and after breathing obstructions. An automatic scoring model trained solely with automatically scored synthetic signals reached good performance on sleep staging (\k{appa}=0.71 and 0.63) and respiratory event segmentation (\k{appa}=0.57 and 0.60), on two test sets consisting of healthy volunteers and OSA patients, respectively. This demonstrates the potential of synthetic data in supporting algorithm development for sleep diagnostics. The source code is available at https://github.com/rikuhuttunen/psg-gan.

2611.24411v1.authors: Huy Q. Nguyen, Benjamin L. Larsen, Luiz C. C. P. Filho, Yijian Meng, Mikael Ø. Lassen, Jonas S. Neergaard-Nielsen, Tobias Gehring, Ulrik L. Andersen, Adnan A. E. Hajomer
2611.24411v1.abstract: Continuous-variable (CV) entanglement offers deterministic generation and room-temperature coherent detection for quantum networks, but distributing it over deployed fibre has been hindered by the need to stabilise optical phase, polarisation, and timing at remote receivers. Here we demonstrate, to our knowledge, the first distribution of CV entanglement over deployed metropolitan fibre using independent coherent receivers. The two modes of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state are delivered to remote nodes through 23 km ($\approx 7$ dB loss) and 450 m ($\approx 1$ dB loss) deployed fibre links. Each node uses its own free-running laser and polarisation-diverse coherent receiver. Co-propagating pilot tones enable digital recovery of timing, phase and polarisation, while inter-mode correlations fix the quadrature alignment. We certify entanglement with a Simon-Duan value of $1.915\pm 0.013$, below the separability bound of 2 and a logarithmic negativity of $0.067\pm0.011$. By replacing optical stabilisation with digital reconstruction, our approach offers a practical route towards scalable CV quantum networks.

2611.24392v1.title: Mesh Sensitivity of Different Boundary Treatments in High-Order Compact Gas-Kinetic Scheme for Hypersonic Heat-Flux Prediction
2611.24392v1.authors: Xingyi Jiang, Jiawang Zhang, Junlei Mu, Xing Ji
2611.24392v1.abstract: Accurate wall-heat-flux prediction in hypersonic flow depends on both the wall treatment and the available near-wall resolution. This work compares three complete implementations of a gas-kinetic scheme (GKS) for Mach~8.03 laminar flow over an isothermal circular cylinder: a linear Green--Gauss scheme (GG), a compact ghost-cell scheme (GC), and a pointwise one-sided compact scheme (POS). In POS, the stationary isothermal-wall conditions are imposed at the two Gaussian points used by the kinetic wall-flux quadrature. A reference mesh and six meshes in the uniform reduction (UR), log-layer unpacked (LLU), and log-layer packed (LLP) families are used to assess heat-flux sensitivity. At 24 digitized experimental angles, GG has the lowest root-mean-square difference on the reference, UR, and LLP families, whereas POS is closest on the two LLU meshes; GC is not the lowest-RMS scheme on any tested mesh. Hence no treatment is uniformly superior. On the present high-aspect-ratio cylinder grids, GG is the more robust choice except under LLU node redistribution, for which POS is preferable. Uniform reduction produces the largest heat-flux response for all three implementations. The comparison concerns complete schemes and does not isolate the pointwise constraints from differences in reconstruction and geometry representation.

2611.24350v1.title: Theses by publication in Spain: output, authorship and integrity concerns
2611.24350v1.authors: Álvaro Cabezas-Clavijo, Nazaret Barriga, Rafael Repiso
2611.24350v1.abstract: Theses by publication are accepted in most Spanish universities, yet there is little empirical evidence on the scientific output that supports them or on the role doctoral candidates play in that output, and it is not even possible to determine what share of all theses defended in the country follow this format. To address this gap, we analysed a sample of 338 theses by publication defended in Spain in 2025 and 2026, identified in the Teseo database and downloaded in full text. On average, each thesis included 4.0 works, of which 3.0 were articles indexed in Scopus, and 61.1% of these articles appeared in first-quartile SJR journals. The doctoral candidate was first author in 81.1% of the articles and held an intermediate position in 12.1%, while 17 candidates (5.4%) were not first or sole author of any article in their compendium. As for publication venues, MDPI was the main publisher, with 23.2% of the articles, and 40.6% of the candidates published at least one work from their compendium with it. Overall, 45.4% of the candidates used so-called grey publishers, such as MDPI or Frontiers, at least once, and for almost 10% of them these publishers were the only outlet for the compendium. We also detected other infrequent but questionable practices, such as the inclusion of works published in journals delisted from Scopus or in special issues guest-edited by the candidates themselves, works still under review, and articles included in two different theses. Taken together, these results point to the need to clarify regulations on theses by publication, in particular regarding the candidate's authorship of the works linked to the thesis and the quality criteria required of publication venues. Theses by publication should also be identified in a standardised way in official registers, so that they can be retrieved and monitored.

2611.24888v1.title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
2611.24888v1.authors: Muhammad Rizky Wellyanto, Hajara-Yasmin Isa, Kexin Xue, Vishal Ravichandran, Wenpeng Lu, Jerry O. Talton, Ranjitha Kumar
2611.24888v1.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

2611.24877v1.title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
2611.24877v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.

2611.24833v1.title: DispersedBFT: Bottleneck-Free Primary-Backup Consensus using Dispersed Replication
2611.24833v1.authors: Nancy Kansal, Celine Sana, Jelle Hellings
2611.24833v1.abstract: The advent of blockchains is fueling the development of novel resilient data management systems (RDSs). Typically, these RDSs are managed using a primary-backup design using a consensus protocol such as PBFT. In these primary-backup designs, a single participant, the primary, is responsible for coordinating the replication and execution of requests. Unfortunately, the central role of the primary makes it a bottleneck that drastically limits performance. In this paper, we propose DispersedBFT, a high performance PBFT-like consensus protocol that utilizes dispersed replication to eliminate the primary bottleneck of PBFT-like consensus. In specific, DispersedBFT uses information dispersal to distribute the task of replicating request from the primary to the backups. We propose several variants of DispersedBFT with either low CPU cost (by using Message Authentication Codes and Merkle proofs) or communication cost (by using digital signatures). We practically analyze the performance of DispersedBFT and show it greatly outperforms PBFT and HotStuff: DispersedBFT supports a throughput of 3.4Mtxn/sec with 43 replicas and is up-to 6.2x faster than PBFT and 2.6x faster than HotStuff.

2611.24823v1.title: One size does not fit all: session-specific effects of deep brain stimulation on hand-motor kinematics in Parkinson's disease
2611.24823v1.authors: Matthias Dold, Joana Pereira, Volker A. Coenen, Bastian Sajonz, Sophia Gimple, Yasin Temel, Marcus L. F. Janssen, Michael Tangermann
2611.24823v1.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) effectively treats motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is unclear whether it changes fine hand movements in the same way for every patient. We analyzed 35 sessions of 19 patients with PD from a multi-center cohort performing the CopyDraw task, a drawing task designed to overcome the subjectivity and limited granularity of clinical assessments. Besides standard kinematics (mean velocity, acceleration, jerk, and drawing accuracy), we derived higher distributional moments and non-linear complexity measures, for 38 features in total. DBS effects were quantified with linear mixed models at the group level and with residualized regression and a random-effects meta-analysis per session. The DBS state was decoded per session with regularized linear discriminant analysis to compare feature sets as behavioral labels for deriving physiomarkers for adaptive DBS (aDBS). DBS modulated all 38 features at the group level, most strongly velocity-related features. However, for every feature, the between-subject variability of the DBS effect exceeded the group-level effect. Only one feature, the detrended fluctuation analysis of the distance to the template, showed a significant mean effect across sessions, and it is not a standard kinematic feature. In six sessions without any significant modulation of standard features, complexity measures were modulated instead. For decoding, standard features alone were the best choice in ten of 35 sessions, but combining all 38 features yielded the highest average area under the ROC curve (0.700 vs. 0.677), with the largest gains in sessions that were hard to decode from standard features. DBS effects on hand-motor behavior are individual. Deriving neural markers for aDBS from behavior therefore requires session-specific analyses with individualized features beyond standard kinematics and group-level effects.

2611.24799v1.title: Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival
2611.24799v1.abstract: Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort. Across a deterministic 5-fold cross-validation pipeline, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of $0.768 \pm 0.068$, while out-of-fold risk stratification yielded significant survival divergence (log-rank $p < 0.001$) accompanied by a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation among high-risk patients. Furthermore, interrogating the network's encoder weights confirmed that the model autonomously recovered canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers of disease progression without supervised feature selection. By demonstrating that systemic failure can be mapped as a geometric phase transition, SOSM establishes a generalizable computational engine for prognostic modeling across biological, industrial and financial complex systems.

2611.24741v1.title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
2611.24741v1.authors: Hiba Akhaddar, Peter Plantinga, Mirco Ravanelli, Tristan Glatard
2611.24741v1.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70\% to 75\% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.

2611.24646v1.authors: Felix Florian Schwald, Martin Meiners, Michael Viehof, Erik Hultman, Edwin Kamau
2611.24646v1.abstract: This paper presents the development of an initial full-vehicle simulation model of the PixKit modular electric test platform in IPG CarMaker. The objective is to create a physics-based and extendable model structure that can serve as a low-level foundation for future digital twin applications. The reference vehicle is a skateboard chassis combining unconventional vehicle characteristics such as four independent wheel-hub motors and rear axle steering capable of high steering angles. Since complete measurement data of the vehicle is not yet available, the model parameterization is based on a combination of manufacturer documentation, derived values and engineering assumptions. The modeling approach focuses on the system-level integration of the main vehicle subsystems rather than on a fully validated representation. The resulting model was assessed through basic driving scenarios with different steering inputs and configurations. The simulations showed stable model behavior and physically plausible interaction between the subsystems. The all-wheel-drive configuration produced symmetric wheel responses in longitudinal driving, while counter-phase rear axle steering increased the yaw response and reduced the simulated turning circle diameter compared with front axle steering only. The circular driving scenario further indicated bounded roll and slip behavior. Overall, the implemented CarMaker model provides a traceable and functional simulation basis for the PixKit vehicle. It can support future model refinement, calibration with real vehicle data and development with the goal of creating a validated digital twin architecture.

2611.24941v1.title: UltraTex: Aligning Physical Knowledge for High-Fidelity PBR Texture Generation
2611.24941v1.authors: Jingzhi Bao, Xiaohe Ma, Hong Li, Yuanming Hu, Xiaoguang Han
2611.24941v1.abstract: Generating physically based rendering (PBR) texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is highly ambiguous, as the observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, and illumination. While current generative methods produce realistic albedo maps, they still struggle to infer accurate metallic and roughness attributes for relighting. We present UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework that moves beyond appearance matching by integrating physical knowledge into multi-view diffusion-based PBR generation. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to generate more detailed albedo maps, and then predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference image, and material semantic priors. To inject material semantics, a lightweight adapter transforms hidden-layer features of a vision-language model (VLM) into intrinsic material representation tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. To model material-light interaction, photometric representation alignment guides intermediate diffusion features toward ground-truth material renderings under controlled lighting. This makes metallic and roughness variations observable through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance for fine-grained material prediction without explicit lighting supervision. Extensive experiments show that UltraTex generates high-quality textures and outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

2611.24940v1.title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
2611.24940v1.authors: Junjie Ye, Yiqi Zhao, Muchen Xu, Celina Shiyu Wang, Hao Dong, Ruohai Ge, Rong Xue, Benjamin J Kolligs, Aditya Dutt, Sasanka Nagavalli, Nassim A. Samad, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh, Yue Wang, Yuliang Guo
2611.24940v1.abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

2611.24939v1.title: Map-Level Inference of Primordial Gravitational Waves from the CMB with Spherical Neural Networks
2611.24939v1.authors: Anto I. Lonappan, Adrian E. Bayer, Brian Keating, Kam Arnold, Giuseppe Puglisi, Ethan O. Nadler
2611.24939v1.abstract: We train a spherical graph convolutional network to infer the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ directly from multifrequency cosmic microwave background (CMB) $B$-mode maps on the cut sky. We test the network on simulations of a generic ground-based experiment including lensed CMB, inhomogeneous noise, and stochastic Galactic dust and synchrotron emission. We compare the network with a multifrequency bandpower likelihood built from the same 20,000 simulations used to train it. Working directly on the maps, with no power-spectrum estimation or component separation, the network reduces the root-mean-square error on $r$ by a factor of 1.3 and gives well-calibrated 68% intervals 1.2 times narrower than the likelihood with the same prior. Saliency maps show that the network learns to favor the deepest regions of the sky and the cleanest frequency channels without being given the survey depth. Both approaches are tied to the foreground model they are built on: the network generalizes to some alternative foreground models without retraining, but not to a three-dimensional dust model with line-of-sight variations. The network can be extended to marginalize over foreground models by training on a broad family, making direct map-level neural inference a promising route to $r$ for future $B$-mode analyses.

2611.24938v1.title: Phoenix: Learning Scene Structure Representations for Generalizable World-Action Models
2611.24938v1.authors: Yupeng Zheng, Chaoyue Li, Linbo Wang, Xiang Li, Yuhang Zheng, Xiaotong Su, Songen Gu, Yichen Zhang, Zebin Xing, Shuai Tian, Jingxiang Guo, Jing Li, Zhiyong Zhao, Zhongpu Xia, Qichao Zhang, Haoran Li, Shuicheng Yan, Dongbin Zhao
2611.24938v1.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.

2611.24937v1.title: LEMUR: A Searchable Web Archive of Deep Chandra Images of Galaxies and Galaxy Clusters
2611.24937v1.authors: Carter L. Rhea, Julie Hlavacek-Larrondo, Marine Prunier, Hyunseop Choi, Megan Donahue, Christian Thibeault
2611.24937v1.abstract: We present LEMUR, a publicly accessible archive of uniformly reduced, deep Chandra images of 2,569 galaxies and galaxy clusters (including groups), comprising 5,505 ACIS observations and 138.8 Ms of exposure. By combining the publicly available imaging observations of each target, we provide background-subtracted, exposure-corrected images in broad, soft, and hard bands at the native ACIS pixel scale of 0.492 arcsec. Our primary goal is to make the wealth of archival Chandra observations accessible to researchers without requiring specialized expertise in X-ray data reduction. 2611.24935v1.authors: Xin Shen, Guangyue Ji, Jie Wang
2611.24935v1.abstract: Chiral spin liquids (CSLs) are paradigmatic fractionalized phases, yet simple exact parent Hamiltonians for them remain scarce. 2611.24929v1.abstract: Prediction models developed from multicenter data are often applied to new centers. A linear mixed model (LMM) captures between-center heterogeneity through random effects. 2611.24939v1.authors: Anto I. Lonappan, Adrian E. Bayer, Brian Keating, Kam Arnold, Giuseppe Puglisi, Ethan O. Nadler

2611.24924v1.authors: Jiahang Lin, Jiahao Chen, Yiding Wang, Shichun Liu, Chengjun Pan, Shihan Dou, Honglin Guo, Yuyang Hu, Changhao Jiang, Zhenhua Han, Hang Yan, Qi Zhang, Tao Gui, Xuanjing Huang
2611.24924v1.abstract: Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. 2611.24914v1.title: The role of externally-driven density fluctuations in the enhancement of beam spray
2611.24914v1.authors: Kyle R. McMillen, Ian D. Min-Roberts, Russell K. Follett, Avram L. Milder, Joseph Katz, Daniel J. Haberberger, Julieta Hernandez Gordillo, Pierre A. Michel, Hans G. Rinderknecht, David Turnbull, John P. Palastro, Dustin H. Froula, Wojciech Rozmus, Jessica L. Shaw
2611.24914v1.abstract: Speckled laser beams, commonly used to ionize and heat plasma for inertial confinement fusion and high-energy-density experiments, are shown to drive long-wavelength plasma-density fluctuations that induce beam spray in other laser beams. Experiments show that a 1053 nm beam undergoes increased beam spray when 351 nm speckled heater beams are on. These observations indicate that the high-intensity speckles sustain an increased level of steady-state density fluctuations. Modeling of these fluctuations predicts amplitudes that are orders of magnitude larger than the level of thermal fluctuations. Beam propagation simulations show increased beam spray due to self-focusing and filamentation when heater-driven density fluctuations are included.

Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.

2611.24901v1.authors: Brian K. Petkov, David R. Klug
2611.24901v1.abstract: We demonstrate for the first time that an optical spectroscopy - electron-vibration-vibration two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy (EVV 2DIR) - has sufficient structural competence to enable the reconstruction of the three-dimensional geometries of drug-protein binding at the level needed for practical drug discovery applications. Klug et al. previously demonstrated experimental detection of drug binding to a kinase using EVV 2DIR. Here we use a quantum mechanical approach to calculate and assign elements of EVV 2DIR spectra for the spectral region 1200-1800 cm$^{-1}$ / 1100-1800 cm$^{-1}$ of 92 protein-ligand complexes. This dataset includes ligand-target poses drawn from existing crystal structures and ligand-target poses created by docking and cofolding models. We find that binding-dependent spectral features are robust, interpretable, and consistent across poses in a given binding mode, and distinct for each unique hydrogen bonding geometry. We construct a spectral distance metric to distinguish poses that conform to the ligand-target hydrogen-bonding pattern of the crystal structure from those that do not. These results show that, given a set of predicted ligand-target poses containing the correct geometry, the hydrogen-bonding pattern of the valid pose may be rapidly identified by comparing simulated and experimental EVV 2DIR spectra. Finally, we discuss the practical implications for a new, high throughput structural biology for drug discovery that will be the subject of forthcoming manuscripts, noting that the base technologies to perform EVV 2DIR quickly and efficiently already exist and will enable a novel structure to be determined in only minutes for each sample. Moreover, this can be achieved without the need for crystallization, isotopic labeling, or low temperatures, non-destructively using picogram quantities of material.

2611.24895v1.title: Efficient search for microlensed gravitational-wave signals with matched filtering and a two-image statistic
2611.24895v1.abstract: Gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences can be microlensed by compact objects along the line of sight, producing frequency-dependent waveform distortions. 2611.24892v1.title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
2611.24892v1.authors: Hengguang Zhou, I-Hung Hsu, Li Chen, Priyanshi Shrivastava, Anastasios Angelopoulos, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ion Stoica, Cho-Jui Hsieh
2611.24892v1.abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. 2611.24885v1.authors: Aleksei V. Ivanov, Christoph Sünderhauf, Jon Kunjummen, Nick S. Blunt, Róbert Izsák
2611.24885v1.abstract: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

2611.24941v1.abstract: Generating physically based rendering (PBR) texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is highly ambiguous, as the observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, and illumination. 2611.24937v1.authors: Carter L. Rhea, Julie Hlavacek-Larrondo, Marine Prunier, Hyunseop Choi, Megan Donahue, Christian Thibeault
2611.24937v1.abstract: We present LEMUR, a publicly accessible archive of uniformly reduced, deep Chandra images of 2,569 galaxies and galaxy clusters (including groups), comprising 5,505 ACIS observations and 138.8 Ms of exposure.
